Next 7 days (Through next Thursday)...

Satellite imagery shows flat ridge over our region while strong 
upper trough was digging south through British Columbia. In the 
meantime, flat westerly flow over our region has resulted in a 
very warm breezy day. Humidity readings are already in the teens 
in the foothills and 20s across many other locations in our CWA. 
Winds have been gusting to near 50 mph frequently in the foothills
near Livingston and 15 to 30 mph across our western zones. A Red 
Flag Warning continues through 9 PM for portions of south central 
Montana and north central and northeastern Wyoming. A few record 
highs are possible this afternoon as well thanks to a prefrontal 
warming environment. 

For tonight, downslope flow will keep it relatively mild most of 
the night. However, a dry cold front will drop into the area late
leading to a switch to northerly upslope winds going into 
Saturday. This will start a cooling trend through the rest of the
weekend.

As the aforementioned upper trough drops into the Pacific NW, we
will see an increasing chance of showers in our far western zones
as a moist southwest flow develops in the mid levels overrunning 
our northeasterly surface flow. Model trends have kept the main 
energy in the trough further west and south than earlier runs, 
delaying atmospheric cooling and the effects of the related upper 
dynamics from reaching our CWA. However, we are confident in 
showers over our western zones thanks to a good moisture fetch in 
the mid level southwest flow. There is enough instability for some
general thunder Saturday afternoon as well, mainly over our 
mountains. 

There does remains notable discrepancy in the ensembles over how 
this system evolves through the weekend and into Monday. While the
models have trended boundary layer temps warmer over the plains,
the chance of significant snowfall remains for the mountains and
foothills due to significant moisture fetch (possibly aided by 
the remnants of Hurricane Rachel). For now, we are becoming more 
confident in seeing colder air move into our far western zones 
Saturday night. Precipitation should change over to all snow in 
the high country and we may see a mix develop in the adjacent 
foothills. The colder air gradually creeps east Sunday into Sunday
night while 500 mb height falls move in and mid level moisture 
flow also increases (EC Extreme Forecast Index indicates a shift 
of tails over our southwest by Sunday). Thus, we expect the 
heaviest precipitation/snowfall to occur later Saturday night 
through Sunday night. Due to the somewhat slower trend of eastward
progression in the models, we have also extended the Winter Storm
Watch through Monday morning. A mix of rain and snow is possible 
out into the plains including Yellowstone County Sunday or Sunday 
evening...though accumulations will be limited, especially for the
river valleys. 

By Monday afternoon, the upper trough weakens and lingers over 
the desert southwest region. The best moisture and accompanying 
dynamics shift east or are cut off from our area as a surface high 
settles over our CWA. However, troughiness aloft may still result
in light pockets of precipitation over the region, but with little
additional impact.

By midweek, ensemble analysis suggest the weakened upper low may
track to our south and swing moisture and ascent into our south 
and eastern zones Wednesday producing a good chance of lower 
elevation showers and mountain snow showers. At the very least,
expect below normal temps and unsettled conditions through
midweek. 

Snow totals...while some uncertainty in timing remains, we  
continue to feel confident the Beartooth/Absaroka and Crazy 
Ranges will see significant snowfall with this system. (70-80% 
chance of 12+ inches above 8k ft). A Winter Storm Watch is in
effect from Saturday night through Monday morning. Snow
accumulation elsewhere will be elevation dependent, especially as
it moves into the plains. For the foothills, snow levels fall to 
under 5k ft late Saturday night from Wheatland to Park Counties, 
and further lower Sunday. We have a 60-90% chance of at least two 
inches at Livingston, Harlowton and Big Timber and also Red Lodge.
The higher hills surrounding Billings may see an inch or two as 
well...though the city itself may struggle to accumulate the wet 
snowfall. Heavy snow is possible along the Melville Foothills on 
the east side of the Crazies, thanks to deep easterly upslope flow
and proximity to the best moisture fetch aloft. We may even need 
to monitor this area for a possible winter storm warning (6+ ins).

Further east, including Sheridan and the Big Horns region, temps
are progged to remain to warm for much accumulating snowfall. 

Overall Precipitation...due to the significant moisture fetch, 
overall precip with this system will be widespread and 
significant. Ensembles show totals of 0.25-0.50" in the east and 
1-1.5" in the west. Western mountains could see more than this,
